task_area: General principles: biochemistry and molecular biology
front: After a carbohydrate meal, liver glycolysis speeds up. Which step is committed, and what slows it when energy is already high?
bottom: Phosphofructokinase-1. ATP and citrate slow it.

bullets.clue: Fructose-6-phosphate becomes fructose-1,6-bisphosphate at this step.
bullets.treat: AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate speed the enzyme. ATP and citrate slow it.
bullets.trap: Naming hexokinase. It is regulated, but it is not the committed step.

source.recommendation: The content outline places pathway regulation in general principles. PFK-1 is the committed step of glycolysis.

diagram.alt: Text card. Phosphofructokinase-1. ATP and citrate slow it.

task_area: General principles: biochemistry and molecular biology
front: During a long fast the liver makes glucose. Which enzymes does glycolysis refuse to run in reverse?
bottom: Pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose-6-phosphatase.

bullets.clue: These four steps are the irreversible ones. The rest of the pathway is shared.
bullets.treat: Biotin is required for pyruvate carboxylase. Glucagon raises fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase activity by lowering fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.
bullets.trap: Saying the whole pathway simply reverses when insulin falls.

source.recommendation: Gluconeogenesis is a general-principles pathway. Only the irreversible enzymes are unique to it.

diagram.alt: Text card. Pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose-6-phosphatase.

task_area: General principles: biochemistry and molecular biology
front: A toddler has lactic acidosis and neurologic injury after carbohydrate loads. Pyruvate, lactate, and alanine are all high.
bottom: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is blocked. Use ketogenic fuel, not more glucose.

bullets.clue: Pyruvate, lactate, and alanine rise together because they share one pool.
bullets.treat: Thiamine is a cofactor. A ketogenic diet bypasses the block.
bullets.trap: Giving more glucose, which only makes more pyruvate that cannot be oxidized.

source.recommendation: PDH links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle. Carbohydrate loading worsens the lactic acidosis.

diagram.alt: Text card. Pyruvate dehydrogenase is blocked. Use ketogenic fuel, not more glucose.

task_area: General principles: biochemistry and molecular biology
front: A poison makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leak protons. Oxygen use rises, ATP falls, and the patient is hot.
bottom: This is an uncoupler. The chain runs, but the gradient makes heat.

bullets.clue: Oxygen consumption is high while ATP is low.
bullets.treat: Separate this from a chain blocker, which stops oxygen use and ATP together.
bullets.trap: Calling every mitochondrial poison a chain inhibitor.

source.recommendation: Uncoupling is a core oxidative-phosphorylation concept. Thermogenin, high-dose aspirin, and dinitrophenol are the classic examples.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is an uncoupler. The chain runs, but the gradient makes heat.

task_area: General principles: biochemistry and molecular biology
front: A man develops dark urine two days after a sulfa drug. The smear shows bite cells and denatured hemoglobin precipitates.
bottom: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase cannot refill NADPH.

bullets.clue: The inheritance is X-linked. Oxidative stress denatures hemoglobin, and the spleen bites the precipitates out.
bullets.treat: Stop the oxidant. An enzyme assay during the hemolysis can look normal, because the oldest cells are already gone.
bullets.trap: Trusting a normal enzyme level drawn on the day of the hemolysis.

source.recommendation: The pentose phosphate pathway is the source of NADPH in red cells. Infection, sulfa drugs, primaquine, and fava beans are typical triggers.

diagram.alt: Text card. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase cannot refill NADPH.

task_area: General principles: biochemistry and molecular biology
front: Bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and corkscrew hairs. The vessels are fragile and collagen will not cross-link.
bottom: Vitamin C is missing. Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need it.

bullets.clue: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine lets collagen form stable triple helices.
bullets.treat: Replace vitamin C. The bleeding is from vessels, not from a missing clotting factor.
bullets.trap: Treating this as vitamin K deficiency because the patient is bleeding.

source.recommendation: Ascorbate is required for collagen hydroxylation. Scurvy is the clinical picture of that missing step.

diagram.alt: Text card. Vitamin C is missing. Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need it.

task_area: General principles: biochemistry and molecular biology
front: A megaloblastic anemia comes with loss of vibration sense. Methylmalonic acid is high and homocysteine is high.
bottom: This is cobalamin deficiency, not folate deficiency alone.

bullets.clue: Both deficiencies stall DNA synthesis. Only cobalamin handles methylmalonyl-CoA.
bullets.treat: Replace B12. Folate alone can improve the anemia and leave the cord injury going.
bullets.trap: Treating a high mean corpuscular volume with folate before the methylmalonic acid is known.

source.recommendation: Methylmalonic acid separates B12 deficiency from folate deficiency. Subacute combined degeneration is the cord finding.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is cobalamin deficiency, not folate deficiency alone.

task_area: General principles: biochemistry and molecular biology
front: A child has a musty body odor, fair skin, and developmental delay. Phenylalanine is high and tyrosine is low.
bottom: Phenylalanine hydroxylase is deficient. Tyrosine is now essential.

bullets.clue: Phenylalanine cannot become tyrosine, so pigment and neurotransmitter precursors fall.
bullets.treat: Restrict phenylalanine and avoid aspartame. Tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency is the variant that also needs neurotransmitter precursors.
bullets.trap: Calling every fair-haired infant with delay a storage disease and missing the diet.

source.recommendation: Phenylketonuria is a core amino-acid pathway. The diet is the treatment that prevents further injury.

diagram.alt: Text card. Phenylalanine hydroxylase is deficient. Tyrosine is now essential.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: An autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 10,000 newborns. About how common are carriers?
bottom: About 1 in 50. The carrier frequency is 2pq.

bullets.clue: Incidence is q squared, so q is 1 in 100. When p is near 1, 2pq is about 1 in 50.
bullets.treat: Use this for counseling in a large population that mates at random and is not under selection.
bullets.trap: Reporting the allele frequency as if it were the carrier frequency.

source.recommendation: Hardy-Weinberg is the quantitative-methods tool the outline expects for carrier estimates.

diagram.alt: Text card. About 1 in 50. The carrier frequency is 2pq.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: A trait shows up in males across generations. Affected men have unaffected sons and carrier daughters.
bottom: X-linked recessive. There is no male-to-male transmission.

bullets.clue: Daughters of affected men are obligate carriers.
bullets.treat: Draw the pedigree before choosing autosomal recessive, which can pass from father to son.
bullets.trap: Calling it autosomal dominant only because more than one generation is affected.

source.recommendation: Transmission pattern is a genetics general principle. Absence of father-to-son transmission is the key.

diagram.alt: Text card. X-linked recessive. There is no male-to-male transmission.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: A child is profoundly hypotonic, then develops insatiable hunger. The paternal copy of 15q is missing or silent.
bottom: Prader-Willi syndrome. The maternal copy of that region is silent.

bullets.clue: The same band from the other parent causes ataxia, inappropriate laughter, and almost no speech.
bullets.treat: Name the parent of origin. The chromosome number alone does not separate the two syndromes.
bullets.trap: Swapping the syndromes because both involve chromosome 15.

source.recommendation: Imprinting is a genetics principle. Prader-Willi needs the paternal contribution. Angelman needs maternal UBE3A.

diagram.alt: Text card. Prader-Willi syndrome. The maternal copy of that region is silent.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: A family has colon cancer and endometrial cancer at young ages. Tumor microsatellites are unstable lengths.
bottom: Lynch syndrome. DNA mismatch repair has failed.

bullets.clue: Microsatellite instability is the footprint of mismatch-repair loss.
bullets.treat: This is not the pathway with hundreds of polyps. That pathway is APC.
bullets.trap: Calling every inherited colon cancer familial adenomatous polyposis.

source.recommendation: Mismatch repair fixes replication errors. Lynch syndrome is the clinical consequence, with colon and endometrial cancer.

diagram.alt: Text card. Lynch syndrome. DNA mismatch repair has failed.

task_area: General principles: human development and genetics
front: A child burns after minutes in the sun and develops skin cancers. Cells cannot clear ultraviolet dimers.
bottom: Nucleotide excision repair has failed.

bullets.clue: Thymine dimers are the lesion. The pathway cuts out a short damaged oligonucleotide.
bullets.treat: Strict sun avoidance follows from the mechanism.
bullets.trap: Confusing this with mismatch repair, which fixes copy errors rather than ultraviolet dimers.

source.recommendation: Xeroderma pigmentosum is the disease of failed nucleotide excision repair.

diagram.alt: Text card. Nucleotide excision repair has failed.

task_area: General principles: biology of tissue response to disease
front: Heart muscle and kidney after a blocked artery show preserved architecture with ghost cells. Brain after ischemia turns to liquid.
bottom: Coagulative necrosis in solid organs. Liquefactive necrosis in the brain.

bullets.clue: Enzymes from the tissue itself digest the brain. Ischemia in heart and kidney denatures those enzymes.
bullets.treat: Name the pattern from the organ. Do not treat every infarct as the same histology.
bullets.trap: Calling brain infarcts coagulative because the cause was ischemia.

source.recommendation: Necrosis patterns are tissue response to injury. Organ of origin predicts the pattern.

diagram.alt: Text card. Coagulative necrosis in solid organs. Liquefactive necrosis in the brain.

task_area: General principles: biology of tissue response to disease
front: A squamous lung cancer presents with severe hypercalcemia. Parathyroid hormone itself is low.
bottom: The tumor is secreting parathyroid hormone-related peptide.

bullets.clue: The peptide mimics the hormone at bone and kidney, so calcium rises and the gland shuts down.
bullets.treat: Treat the calcium and the cancer. Do not operate on a normal parathyroid.
bullets.trap: Sending the patient for parathyroidectomy because the calcium is high.

source.recommendation: Paraneoplastic PTHrP is a classic squamous-cell product. Suppressed native PTH separates it from primary hyperparathyroidism.

diagram.alt: Text card. The tumor is secreting parathyroid hormone-related peptide.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A drug binds the same pocket as the substrate. More substrate restores the maximum velocity. Apparent Km rises.
bottom: Competitive inhibition. Vmax is unchanged.

bullets.clue: On a double-reciprocal plot the lines meet on the y-axis, because 1 over Vmax is the same.
bullets.treat: A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax and does not yield to more substrate.
bullets.trap: Saying every inhibitor lowers the maximum velocity.

source.recommendation: Competitive versus noncompetitive inhibition is a pharmacodynamics principle on the outline.

diagram.alt: Text card. Competitive inhibition. Vmax is unchanged.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A patient in status epilepticus needs a therapeutic level now. Maintenance dosing would take many half-lives.
bottom: Give a loading dose. It depends on volume of distribution, not clearance.

bullets.clue: Loading dose is target concentration times volume, divided by bioavailability.
bullets.treat: Clearance sets the maintenance rate. Volume sets the size of the first dose.
bullets.trap: Raising the drip and waiting. Steady state still takes about four half-lives.

source.recommendation: Loading versus maintenance dose is a core pharmacokinetic distinction.

diagram.alt: Text card. Give a loading dose. It depends on volume of distribution, not clearance.

task_area: General principles: pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic processes
front: A drug's half-life grows longer as the level rises. A constant amount, not a constant fraction, leaves each hour.
bottom: Elimination is zero order. The enzymes are saturated.

bullets.clue: Phenytoin, ethanol, and high-dose aspirin are the usual examples.
bullets.treat: Small dose changes can cause large level changes once the pathway is full.
bullets.trap: Using one fixed half-life to time the next blood level.

source.recommendation: Zero-order kinetics is a pharmacokinetics principle. Saturated enzymes remove a fixed amount per unit time.

diagram.alt: Text card. Elimination is zero order. The enzymes are saturated.

front: Damaged DNA should stop a cell before it copies that DNA. One protein halts G1. Another holds the transcription factor until it is phosphorylated.
bottom: p53 halts G1. Hypophosphorylated Rb holds E2F.

bullets.clue: p53 raises p21, which keeps the kinase from phosphorylating Rb.
bullets.treat: Loss of either brake allows a damaged cell to divide. Rb loss is shared by retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma.
bullets.trap: Saying p53 directly phosphorylates Rb.

source.recommendation: Cell-cycle checkpoints are general cell biology. p53 and Rb are the two brakes tested most often.

diagram.alt: Text card. p53 halts G1. Hypophosphorylated Rb holds E2F.

front: A secreted bacterial protein causes disease at very low dose, may be encoded by a phage, and is destroyed by heat. The wall lipid does the opposite.
bottom: Exotoxin versus endotoxin.

bullets.clue: Endotoxin is lipopolysaccharide. It is heat stable and drives fever through interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor.
bullets.treat: Exotoxins are proteins with specific mechanisms. Endotoxin is the gram-negative wall.
bullets.trap: Calling every fever-producing bacterial product an exotoxin.

source.recommendation: The outline separates toxin biology from the organism list. Heat stability and chemistry tell them apart.

diagram.alt: Contrast. Exotoxin versus endotoxin.

front: An enveloped virus uses one surface protein to find CD4 and a chemokine receptor, and a second protein to fuse.
bottom: gp120 binds. gp41 fuses.

bullets.clue: The chemokine receptor is CCR5 early and CXCR4 later.
bullets.treat: A fusion inhibitor targets gp41. A receptor blocker targets CCR5. They are not the same drug.
bullets.trap: Swapping the two proteins, or treating every HIV drug as a reverse-transcriptase inhibitor.

source.recommendation: HIV entry is a microbial-biology and pharmacology junction. Binding and fusion are different steps.

diagram.alt: Text card. gp120 binds. gp41 fuses.

front: A child has repeated infections with staphylococci and aspergillus, and a test of oxidative burst does not turn blue.
bottom: NADPH oxidase is missing. Catalase-positive organisms survive inside the phagocyte.

bullets.clue: The burst is what kills organisms that bring their own catalase.
bullets.treat: Protect against those organisms. The nitroblue tetrazolium or dihydrorhodamine test shows the missing burst.
bullets.trap: Blaming antibodies. B cells are intact. The phagocyte cannot finish the kill.

source.recommendation: Chronic granulomatous disease is failed NADPH oxidase. Catalase-positive organisms are the clinical clue.

diagram.alt: Text card. NADPH oxidase is missing. Catalase-positive organisms survive inside the phagocyte.

front: Recurrent Neisseria infections start in adolescence. The membrane-attack complex cannot form.
bottom: Terminal complement, C5 through C9, is missing.

bullets.clue: The same risk appears in a patient treated with a C5 inhibitor.
bullets.treat: Vaccinate against meningococcus and treat infections promptly. Earlier complement defects look different and often include immune-complex disease.
bullets.trap: Calling every complement problem a terminal-complex problem.

source.recommendation: The membrane-attack complex is the shared defense against Neisseria. That is the immune-response fact.

diagram.alt: Text card. Terminal complement, C5 through C9, is missing.

front: A boy has very high IgM, almost no IgG or IgA, and Pneumocystis. His T cells cannot signal B cells to switch class.
bottom: CD40 ligand is missing.

bullets.clue: Without that signal, B cells stay on IgM.
bullets.treat: This is cell-mediated failure as well as antibody failure, which is why Pneumocystis appears.
bullets.trap: Calling it isolated agammaglobulinemia. Those patients lack B cells and do not have this opportunistic pattern.

source.recommendation: Hyper-IgM syndrome is failed class switching from a missing CD40 ligand, usually X-linked.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. CD40 ligand is missing.

front: After six months of age a boy has recurrent bacterial infections, no tonsils, and no B cells. Viral infections are handled normally.
bottom: Bruton tyrosine kinase is missing. B cells never mature.

bullets.clue: T cells are intact, so viruses and fungi are less of the story.
bullets.treat: Give immunoglobulin. Do not expect lymphoid tissue on exam.
bullets.trap: Confusing this with a combined deficiency, which loses T-cell function too.

source.recommendation: X-linked agammaglobulinemia presents after maternal IgG fades. The missing tissue is B-cell tissue.

diagram.alt: Text card. Bruton tyrosine kinase is missing. B cells never mature.

front: An infant has low calcium, no thymic shadow, and a conotruncal heart defect.
bottom: The third and fourth pharyngeal pouches did not form.

bullets.clue: Those pouches make the inferior parathyroids and the thymus. Neural-crest cells also fail the outflow tract.
bullets.treat: Protect from live vaccines and irradiated blood until the immune defect is defined. Calcium and the heart need their own care.
bullets.trap: Calling this a pharyngeal-arch cartilage problem. The pouches, not the arch cartilages, are the missing parts.

source.recommendation: DiGeorge syndrome is a third-and-fourth pouch field defect. Hypocalcemia, no thymus, and outflow-tract defects travel together.

diagram.alt: Text card. The third and fourth pharyngeal pouches did not form.

front: Sudden swelling of the face and airway with no urticaria, often after a dental procedure. Complement C4 is low all the time.
bottom: C1 inhibitor is missing or not working.

bullets.clue: The pathway that makes bradykinin is unchecked. Histamine is not the mediator.
bullets.treat: Airway threats need a bradykinin-pathway drug, not the allergy algorithm alone.
bullets.trap: Giving epinephrine and antihistamines and considering the problem solved.

source.recommendation: Hereditary angioedema is a complement regulatory disease. Low C4 between attacks is the screening clue.

diagram.alt: Text card. C1 inhibitor is missing or not working.

front: A tired patient has a low ferritin, a high iron-binding capacity, and a low serum iron. Another anemic patient has low iron but a low binding capacity and a normal or high ferritin.
bottom: The first is iron deficiency. The second is anemia of chronic disease.

bullets.clue: Ferritin is the storage marker that separates them. Binding capacity rises only when stores are empty.
bullets.treat: Replace iron when stores are empty. Treat the underlying disease when stores are locked away.
bullets.trap: Giving iron to every low serum iron. Chronic disease already has iron the marrow cannot use.

source.recommendation: Iron studies separate deficiency from anemia of inflammation. That pairing is a blood-system essential.

diagram.alt: Text card. The first is iron deficiency. The second is anemia of chronic disease.

front: Red cells sickle when oxygen falls. Acid, dehydration, and a high cell hemoglobin concentration make it worse.
bottom: Deoxyhemoglobin S polymerizes.

bullets.clue: The polymer distorts the cell, which then occludes small vessels and hemolyzes.
bullets.treat: Oxygen, fluids, and pain control for a crisis. Hydroxyurea raises hemoglobin F over time.
bullets.trap: Treating the shape change as an antibody problem.

source.recommendation: Sickling is a hemoglobin polymerization disease. Hypoxia, acidosis, and high mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration favor the polymer.

diagram.alt: Text card. Deoxyhemoglobin S polymerizes.

front: A family has anemia, spherical red cells, and a spleen that is doing too much. After the spleen is removed the anemia improves and encapsulated bacteria become the risk.
bottom: The membrane scaffold, often ankyrin or spectrin, is weak.

bullets.clue: The spleen traps the poorly deformable spheres. Parvovirus can suddenly stop red-cell production.
bullets.treat: Folate supports the high turnover. Splenectomy helps the anemia and then requires vaccine protection.
bullets.trap: Removing the spleen and forgetting the infection risk that follows.

source.recommendation: Hereditary spherocytosis is a red-cell membrane disease. Splenectomy trades hemolysis for encapsulated-organism risk.

diagram.alt: Steps. The membrane scaffold, often ankyrin or spectrin, is weak.

front: Mild mucosal bleeding, a normal platelet count, and a normal or slightly long PTT. The factor VIII carrier protein is low.
bottom: von Willebrand factor is low or not working.

bullets.clue: It carries factor VIII and sticks platelets to collagen. The platelet count itself is normal.
bullets.treat: Desmopressin helps many patients with type 1 disease. It is the wrong drug when the factor binds platelets too tightly.
bullets.trap: Transfusing platelets for a normal count.

source.recommendation: von Willebrand disease is the common inherited mucocutaneous bleeding disorder. The count is not the defect.

diagram.alt: Text card. von Willebrand factor is low or not working.

front: A boy has hemarthroses. PTT is long, PT is normal, and the bleeding corrects when factor VIII is added.
bottom: Factor VIII is missing.

bullets.clue: The inheritance is X-linked. Factor IX deficiency looks similar and does not correct with factor VIII.
bullets.treat: Replace the missing factor. Desmopressin can help mild factor VIII deficiency, not factor IX deficiency.
bullets.trap: Giving vitamin K for an intrinsic-pathway bleeding disorder.

source.recommendation: Hemophilia A is factor VIII. The joint bleeding and the isolated PTT prolongation are the picture.

diagram.alt: Text card. Factor VIII is missing.

front: A middle-aged adult has a very high neutrophil count, a low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, and a chromosome swap between 9 and 22.
bottom: BCR-ABL is driving the marrow.

bullets.clue: A reactive neutrophil count has a high alkaline phosphatase and no Philadelphia chromosome.
bullets.treat: A tyrosine kinase inhibitor targets the fusion. Blast crisis means the disease has left the chronic phase.
bullets.trap: Calling every extreme neutrophil count a leukemia.

source.recommendation: Chronic myeloid leukemia is defined by BCR-ABL. The alkaline phosphatase separates it from a leukemoid reaction.

diagram.alt: Text card. BCR-ABL is driving the marrow.

front: A patient treats the physician as if the physician were a critical parent. The feeling belongs to an earlier relationship.
bottom: This is transference.

bullets.clue: Countertransference is the physician's feeling about the patient.
bullets.treat: Notice it and keep the boundary. Do not act out the old relationship.
bullets.trap: Using the two words for the same direction of feeling.

source.recommendation: Transference and countertransference are communication concepts on the behavioral-health outline.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is transference.

front: A patient drinks heavily, agrees it is a problem, and has not decided to change.
bottom: This is contemplation, not action.

bullets.clue: Precontemplation does not yet see a problem. Preparation has a plan. Action has started the change.
bullets.treat: Match the conversation to the stage. Arguing with someone who does not see a problem hardens it.
bullets.trap: Handing a quit plan to a person who does not believe there is anything to quit.

source.recommendation: Stages of change are a behavioral principle. The intervention has to match the stage.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is contemplation, not action.

front: One weak limb is stiff, with brisk reflexes and an upgoing toe. Another is flaccid, wasted, and fasciculating, with quiet reflexes.
bottom: The first is an upper motor neuron. The second is a lower motor neuron.

bullets.clue: Upper motor neurons inhibit the reflex arc. Their loss releases it.
bullets.treat: Localize before you image. A mixed picture can be both, as in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
bullets.trap: Calling every weak limb a stroke.

source.recommendation: The motor-neuron signs are a nervous-system localization rule used throughout the outline.

diagram.alt: Text card. The first is an upper motor neuron. The second is a lower motor neuron.

front: Sudden weakness of the face and arm, with little leg weakness, and the patient cannot find words. The other pattern is a weak leg with preserved speech.
bottom: The first is the middle cerebral artery. The second is the anterior cerebral artery.

bullets.clue: The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral cortex. The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial leg area.
bullets.treat: A visual-field cut with little weakness points at the posterior cerebral artery instead.
bullets.trap: Treating every hemiparesis as the same arterial territory.

source.recommendation: Arterial territories are nervous-system anatomy. Face and arm versus leg is the bedside split.

diagram.alt: Text card. The first is the middle cerebral artery. The second is the anterior cerebral artery.

front: One side of the body is weak and has lost vibration. Pain and temperature are lost on the other side, a level below the injury.
bottom: Half of the cord is cut.

bullets.clue: The spinothalamic fibers have already crossed. The corticospinal and dorsal columns have not.
bullets.treat: Image the cord. A one-sided cord lesion is not a brain lesion.
bullets.trap: Sending the patient for a head scan only, because the findings are on both sides of the body.

source.recommendation: Brown-Sequard physiology follows from which tracts have crossed. That is spinal cord anatomy.

diagram.alt: Text card. Half of the cord is cut.

front: A patient loses pain and temperature on one side of the face and the opposite side of the body, with a small pupil, a drooping lid, and ataxia. Strength is spared.
bottom: The lateral medulla is infarcted.

bullets.clue: The spinal trigeminal nucleus, the spinothalamic tract, sympathetic fibers, and the inferior cerebellar peduncle sit there.
bullets.treat: The usual vessel is the vertebral artery or its posterior inferior cerebellar branch.
bullets.trap: Calling it a capsular stroke because the face and body are both involved. Power is spared here.

source.recommendation: Lateral medullary syndrome is a brainstem localization. Crossed sensory loss plus Horner syndrome is the pattern.

diagram.alt: Text card. The lateral medulla is infarcted.

front: Speech is fluent, full of wrong words, and the patient does not understand what is said. There is no arm weakness.
bottom: The posterior superior temporal lobe is injured.

bullets.clue: Comprehension and repetition fail. The nearby motor cortex is spared, so the arm is strong.
bullets.treat: The nonfluent pattern, with intact comprehension and a weak arm, sits in the frontal lobe instead.
bullets.trap: Calling every aphasia a frontal lesion.

source.recommendation: Wernicke aphasia is a dominant temporal lesion. Fluency with failed comprehension is the bedside split.

diagram.alt: Text card. The posterior superior temporal lobe is injured.

front: Resting tremor, rigidity, and slow movement. Pigmented cells in the midbrain are gone, and the protein aggregates are alpha-synuclein.
bottom: The nigrostriatal dopamine projection has died.

bullets.clue: Those cells live in the substantia nigra pars compacta and project to the striatum.
bullets.treat: Replacing dopamine effect helps movement. It does not rebuild the cells.
bullets.trap: Localizing the loss to the striatum itself. The striatum is the target, not the source.

source.recommendation: Parkinson disease is loss of substantia nigra pars compacta neurons. Lewy bodies contain alpha-synuclein.

diagram.alt: Text card. The nigrostriatal dopamine projection has died.

front: A young adult has neurologic symptoms separated in time and place. Spinal fluid has unmatched oligoclonal bands, and the cells that make central myelin are the ones injured.
bottom: Oligodendrocytes are being attacked.

bullets.clue: Oligoclonal bands are antibodies made inside the nervous system, not a copy of the serum.
bullets.treat: Separate this from a peripheral myelin disease, which is Schwann cells and has no oligoclonal bands of this kind.
bullets.trap: Blaming Schwann cells because the problem is myelin.

source.recommendation: Multiple sclerosis targets oligodendrocytes. Oligoclonal bands support an immune process inside the central nervous system.

diagram.alt: Text card. Oligodendrocytes are being attacked.

front: After a temple blow the patient wakes, then declines. The bleed on the scan is lens shaped and does not cross suture lines.
bottom: The middle meningeal artery has torn.

bullets.clue: That artery runs under the pterion in the epidural space. The dura is stuck at the sutures.
bullets.treat: This is a surgical emergency. A crescent that crosses sutures is bridging-vein blood in the subdural space instead.
bullets.trap: Calling every post-traumatic bleed a subdural hematoma.

source.recommendation: Epidural hematoma is arterial blood from the middle meningeal artery. The lens shape and the lucid interval are the classic clues.

diagram.alt: Text card. The middle meningeal artery has torn.

front: A pigmented spot is asymmetric, has an irregular border, more than one color, and has been growing.
bottom: This is melanoma, and thickness is the main local prognostic number.

bullets.clue: Depth of invasion, not the width of the spot, dominates prognosis for a localized lesion.
bullets.treat: Excise with a margin guided by that thickness. Do not shave it and lose the depth.
bullets.trap: Reassuring the patient from the diameter alone.

source.recommendation: Melanoma recognition uses the asymmetry, border, color, and change. Breslow thickness guides prognosis.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is melanoma, and thickness is the main local prognostic number.

front: Flaccid blisters and oral erosions. A rubbing finger shears the skin. Antibody light surrounds each keratinocyte.
bottom: Desmoglein is the target. The split is inside the epidermis.

bullets.clue: The cells lose their attachments to each other and look like a row of tombstones.
bullets.treat: The tense, intact blisters of an older adult, with a line of antibody along the basement membrane, are a different disease.
bullets.trap: Using one treatment plan for every blistering rash.

source.recommendation: Pemphigus vulgaris is an intraepidermal, desmoglein disease. Nikolsky sign and the net-like antibody pattern are the clues.

diagram.alt: Text card. Desmoglein is the target. The split is inside the epidermis.

front: Pain and bony enlargement of the farthest finger joints, worse with use, with no prolonged morning stiffness and no hot swollen wrists.
bottom: This is osteoarthritis.

bullets.clue: The cartilage is worn. Osteophytes at the distal joints are Heberden nodes.
bullets.treat: The pattern that hits the knuckles and proximal finger joints, with more than an hour of morning stiffness, is inflammatory instead.
bullets.trap: Starting a disease-modifying drug for mechanical joint wear.

source.recommendation: Osteoarthritis favors distal finger joints and use-related pain. That distribution separates it from rheumatoid arthritis.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is osteoarthritis.

front: A teenager has night pain in a long bone, relieved a little by anti-inflammatory drugs. The film shows a sunburst at the metaphysis and a lifted periosteum.
bottom: This is osteosarcoma.

bullets.clue: The tumor makes bone. Loss of the Rb brake is a recognized association.
bullets.treat: A diaphyseal tumor with onion-skin periosteum in the same age group is a different small round cell tumor.
bullets.trap: Calling every pediatric bone tumor a cyst because the patient is young.

source.recommendation: Osteosarcoma arises at the metaphysis of long bones. Sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman triangle are the film clues.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is osteosarcoma.

front: Needle-shaped crystals from a hot joint are yellow when they lie parallel to the compensator.
bottom: The crystal is monosodium urate, and the birefringence is negative.

bullets.clue: Rhomboid crystals that are blue when parallel are calcium pyrophosphate.
bullets.treat: The color depends on orientation. Read it against the compensator, not from the shape alone.
bullets.trap: Calling every crystal in a joint gout.

source.recommendation: Gout crystals are negatively birefringent needles. Pseudogout crystals are positively birefringent rhomboids.

diagram.alt: Text card. The crystal is monosodium urate, and the birefringence is negative.

front: A boy uses his hands to walk up his own legs, has large calves that are not strong, and an X-linked frameshift that erases a membrane protein.
bottom: Dystrophin is absent.

bullets.clue: The calves are pseudohypertrophy from fat and fibrosis. A truncated protein, rather than none, is the milder allelic disease.
bullets.treat: Supportive care and the newer genetic therapies depend on whether any reading frame remains.
bullets.trap: Calling the calves true muscle hypertrophy.

source.recommendation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked frameshift of dystrophin. Gowers sign and calf pseudohypertrophy are the clues.

diagram.alt: Text card. Dystrophin is absent.

front: A cyanotic infant has a boot-shaped heart, a ventricular septal defect, right ventricular thickening, an overriding aorta, and a narrowed pulmonary outflow.
bottom: These four lesions are the tetralogy.

bullets.clue: Squatting raises systemic resistance and sends more blood to the lungs.
bullets.treat: The outflow-tract mistake is a neural-crest problem, which is why the lesions travel with other crest defects.
bullets.trap: Treating the cyanosis as a lung disease and missing the shunt.

source.recommendation: Tetralogy of Fallot is pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta, and a ventricular septal defect.

diagram.alt: Text card. These four lesions are the tetralogy.

front: A preterm infant has a continuous murmur and bounding pulses. The vessel that should have closed is being held open by a prostaglandin.
bottom: Close a patent ductus arteriosus with a prostaglandin inhibitor.

bullets.clue: Indomethacin or ibuprofen reduces the prostaglandin that keeps the duct open.
bullets.treat: The opposite move, a prostaglandin infusion, is for a duct-dependent lesion that needs the vessel open.
bullets.trap: Closing every ductus. Some cyanotic lesions die if you do.

source.recommendation: A preterm patent ductus is kept open by prostaglandin E. Inhibiting that synthesis closes it.

diagram.alt: Text card. Close a patent ductus arteriosus with a prostaglandin inhibitor.

front: A crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiates to the carotids. The carotid upstroke is slow and weak.
bottom: The aortic valve is stenotic.

bullets.clue: The three late symptoms are angina, syncope, and dyspnea from the failed left ventricle.
bullets.treat: A holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla is mitral regurgitation instead.
bullets.trap: Calling every systolic murmur aortic stenosis.

source.recommendation: Aortic stenosis is heard at the right upper sternal border and radiates to the carotids, with pulsus parvus et tardus.

diagram.alt: Text card. The aortic valve is stenotic.

front: Several days after a myocardial infarction the patient suddenly dies. Macrophages have cleared dead muscle and the wall is soft.
bottom: Rupture is most likely from about day 3 to day 7.

bullets.clue: Neutrophils arrive in the first days. Macrophages follow and remove debris before a scar exists.
bullets.treat: A new holosystolic murmur in that window can be a ruptured papillary muscle or a septal defect, not only free-wall rupture.
bullets.trap: Expecting a histologic change in the first hour. The first hours show nothing on light microscopy.

source.recommendation: The infarction timeline is cardiovascular pathology. The soft wall of days 3 to 7 is when rupture occurs.

diagram.alt: Text card. Rupture is most likely from about day 3 to day 7.

front: Hypotension, distended neck veins, and quiet heart sounds after trauma. Diastolic pressures in the heart chambers equalize, and the arterial pressure falls more than expected on inspiration.
bottom: Fluid under pressure is compressing the heart.

bullets.clue: The y descent is lost. The electrocardiogram may alternate in voltage.
bullets.treat: Drain the pericardium. More preload helps only as a bridge.
bullets.trap: Giving a diuretic because the neck veins are up.

source.recommendation: Tamponade is equalization of diastolic pressures, pulsus paradoxus, and Beck's triad of hypotension, distended veins, and muffled sounds.

diagram.alt: Text card. Fluid under pressure is compressing the heart.

front: One calcium-channel blocker swells the ankles and can speed the heart. Another slows the heart and should not be stacked on a beta blocker.
bottom: The first is a dihydropyridine. The second acts on the heart.

bullets.clue: Amlodipine and nifedipine prefer vessels. Verapamil and diltiazem prefer the node and the myocardium.
bullets.treat: Do not combine a heart-rate-lowering calcium blocker with a beta blocker.
bullets.trap: Using a short-acting dihydropyridine alone in an acute coronary syndrome.

source.recommendation: Dihydropyridines vasodilate. Non-dihydropyridines slow the heart. That split prevents a dangerous combination.

diagram.alt: Text card. The first is a dihydropyridine. The second acts on the heart.

front: A drug blocks the sodium-potassium pump, raises vagal tone, and in excess causes yellow vision and almost any arrhythmia. A low potassium makes binding easier.
bottom: This is digoxin toxicity.

bullets.clue: The same pump block is the therapeutic effect at a lower level.
bullets.treat: Give the specific antibody fragment for serious toxicity. Correct potassium carefully.
bullets.trap: Treating the visual change as an eye disease.

source.recommendation: Digoxin inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase. Hypokalemia increases binding and toxicity.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is digoxin toxicity.

front: A clot stops blood flow to ventilated lung. Another disease fills alveoli so blood passes them with no air. Extra oxygen barely helps the second one.
bottom: The clot is dead space. The filled alveoli are shunt.

bullets.clue: Dead space is ventilation without perfusion. Shunt is perfusion without ventilation.
bullets.treat: Oxygen helps a high ventilation-perfusion mismatch more than it helps a true shunt.
bullets.trap: Turning up oxygen and expecting a shunt to correct fully.

source.recommendation: Pulmonary physiology separates dead space from shunt by whether oxygen can reach the blood.

diagram.alt: Text card. The clot is dead space. The filled alveoli are shunt.

front: A rise in carbon dioxide, acid, temperature, or 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate shifts the oxygen curve.
bottom: The shift is to the right, and hemoglobin unloads oxygen.

bullets.clue: A right shift raises the partial pressure needed for a given saturation.
bullets.treat: Fetal hemoglobin and a left shift hold oxygen tighter, which is useful before birth and costly in tissue.
bullets.trap: Saying a right shift means hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly.

source.recommendation: The oxyhemoglobin curve shifts right when tissues need oxygen. Carbon dioxide, acid, heat, and 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate do that.

diagram.alt: Text card. The shift is to the right, and hemoglobin unloads oxygen.

front: A premature infant grunts and retracts. The cells that make the surface-tension film are immature, and the lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio is low.
bottom: Surfactant is missing.

bullets.clue: Type II cells make dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine, which lowers surface tension so alveoli stay open.
bullets.treat: Maternal corticosteroids before a preterm birth speed that film. After birth the infant needs support and often replacement.
bullets.trap: Treating the retractions as infection only and missing the lung mechanics.

source.recommendation: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is surfactant deficiency. The lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio estimates lung maturity.

diagram.alt: Text card. Surfactant is missing.

front: A nonsmoking adult has basilar emphysema and liver disease. The protein that should inhibit elastase is low, and the liver is holding an abnormal form of it.
bottom: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is deficient and trapped in hepatocytes.

bullets.clue: Unopposed elastase destroys alveolar walls, worse at the bases.
bullets.treat: Smoking accelerates the lung injury and is worth stopping for that reason alone.
bullets.trap: Attributing every early emphysema to tobacco without asking about the liver.

source.recommendation: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes panacinar emphysema and liver retention of the misfolded protein.

diagram.alt: Text card. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is deficient and trapped in hepatocytes.

front: Low oxygen in a region of lung constricts the local arterioles. Years of that constriction raise the pressure the right heart must pump against.
bottom: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.

bullets.clue: The reflex sends blood toward better-ventilated lung. Chronic hypoxia makes the vessels remodel.
bullets.treat: Oxygen is the treatment that relaxes those vessels. A left-heart cause of pulmonary hypertension will not respond the same way.
bullets.trap: Giving a systemic vasodilator and expecting only the lung vessels to relax.

source.recommendation: Hypoxic vasoconstriction is protective in one region and a cause of right-heart strain when the whole lung is hypoxic.

diagram.alt: Text card. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.

front: A curved gastric organism splits urea and alkalinizes its niche. It is linked to duodenal ulcer, a lymphoma of mucosa-associated tissue, and gastric adenocarcinoma.
bottom: The organism makes urease.

bullets.clue: Ammonia from urea buffers the acid so the organism can live.
bullets.treat: Eradication treats the ulcer and can regress the low-grade lymphoma. It does not reverse an invasive adenocarcinoma.
bullets.trap: Treating the lymphoma with eradication after it has already transformed and invaded.

source.recommendation: Helicobacter pylori urease is both the survival trick and the basis of the breath test.

diagram.alt: Text card. The organism makes urease.

front: Mild unconjugated bilirubin rises during a fast or a viral illness, with no hemolysis and a normal exam. The enzyme is reduced, not absent.
bottom: This is the mild glucuronosyltransferase deficiency.

bullets.clue: Complete absence of the enzyme in an infant causes severe unconjugated jaundice and the risk of kernicterus.
bullets.treat: Reassure the mild adult form. The severe infant form needs a different plan, including light and transplant consideration.
bullets.trap: Starting a hemolysis workup for every unconjugated rise and never asking about fasting.

source.recommendation: Gilbert syndrome is a partial bilirubin-conjugation defect that shows up under stress. Crigler-Najjar type I is absence of the enzyme.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. This is the mild glucuronosyltransferase deficiency.

front: Portal pressure rises. Veins that should have been separate now meet at the lower esophagus, around the umbilicus, and in the rectum.
bottom: Those meetings are the portosystemic anastomoses.

bullets.clue: Left gastric meets azygos at the esophagus. Paraumbilical veins meet the abdominal wall. Superior rectal meets the middle and inferior rectal veins.
bullets.treat: Bleeding from the esophageal meeting is the one that kills. The others explain the physical findings.
bullets.trap: Calling hemorrhoids a sign of portal hypertension in every patient. Most hemorrhoids are not.

source.recommendation: Portal hypertension opens embryologic connections between portal and systemic veins. Esophageal varices are the dangerous one.

diagram.alt: Text card. Those meetings are the portosystemic anastomoses.

front: Chronic diarrhea, iron deficiency, and an intensely itchy blistering rash. The flattened villi are worst in the distal duodenum, and the antibody is against tissue transglutaminase.
bottom: Gluten is driving an immune injury in a person with HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8.

bullets.clue: The rash is dermatitis herpetiformis, IgA at the dermal papillae.
bullets.treat: Confirm while the patient is still eating gluten. A gluten-free diet started first can make the tests go quiet.
bullets.trap: Diagnosing from symptoms and stopping gluten before the tests.

source.recommendation: Celiac disease injures proximal small bowel in people with HLA-DQ2 or DQ8. Tissue-transglutaminase IgA is the serology.

diagram.alt: Text card. Gluten is driving an immune injury in a person with HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8.

front: A newborn does not pass meconium. The distal bowel has no ganglion cells, and a finger exam is followed by a squirt of stool.
bottom: Neural crest cells never reached the distal colon.

bullets.clue: The aganglionic segment stays contracted. The normal bowel upstream dilates.
bullets.treat: The association with Down syndrome is real, but most affected infants do not have it.
bullets.trap: Calling every delayed meconium cystic fibrosis. That disease plugs the lumen. The wall here has no neurons.

source.recommendation: Hirschsprung disease is failed neural-crest migration. The biopsy shows no ganglion cells in the distal bowel.

diagram.alt: Text card. Neural crest cells never reached the distal colon.

front: A young adult has liver disease, a movement disorder, and a brown ring at the edge of the cornea. Ceruloplasmin is low.
bottom: Copper cannot be excreted into bile.

bullets.clue: The transporter is ATP7B. Copper deposits in liver, basal ganglia, and Descemet membrane.
bullets.treat: Chelation or zinc is the medical treatment. A low ceruloplasmin supports the diagnosis and is not itself the disease.
bullets.trap: Treating the tremor as primary Parkinson disease.

source.recommendation: Wilson disease is ATP7B failure. Kayser-Fleischer rings, a low ceruloplasmin, and liver disease are the triad.

diagram.alt: Text card. Copper cannot be excreted into bile.

front: Low kidney perfusion releases renin. A lung enzyme makes angiotensin II, which prefers the efferent arteriole and asks the adrenal for aldosterone.
bottom: This is the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone sequence.

bullets.clue: Juxtaglomerular cells make renin. The liver makes angiotensinogen. Aldosterone saves sodium and spills potassium in the principal cell.
bullets.treat: Blocking the converting enzyme lowers the glomerular pressure behind a soft efferent arteriole, which is why creatinine can rise.
bullets.trap: Putting antidiuretic hormone in this sequence. It is a different axis.

source.recommendation: Renin, angiotensin-converting enzyme, angiotensin II, and aldosterone are the volume axis. Each step has its own drug.

diagram.alt: Text card. This is the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone sequence.

front: The urine cannot be acidified below 5.5, potassium is low, and kidney stones form. A different acidosis has a high potassium and a low renin or a low aldosterone effect.
bottom: The first is distal renal tubular acidosis. The second is the low-aldosterone type.

bullets.clue: Distal cells fail to secrete hydrogen. The hyperkalemic type fails because aldosterone is missing or blocked.
bullets.treat: Potassium tells them apart. Do not replace potassium blindly without knowing which acidosis you have.
bullets.trap: Calling every normal-anion-gap acidosis diarrhea. Diarrhea can acidify the urine.

source.recommendation: Type 1 renal tubular acidosis cannot acidify the urine and wastes potassium. Type 4 retains potassium.

diagram.alt: Text card. The first is distal renal tubular acidosis. The second is the low-aldosterone type.

front: Muddy brown casts in the urine. In another patient, white-cell casts. In a third, red-cell casts.
bottom: Tubular injury, interstitial or pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis, in that order.

bullets.clue: The cast is a mold of the nephron, so its contents point at the compartment.
bullets.treat: Fatty casts and heavy protein point at the nephrotic pattern instead.
bullets.trap: Treating every cast as infection.

source.recommendation: Urine microscopy localizes kidney injury. The cast contents name the compartment.

diagram.alt: Text card. Tubular injury, interstitial or pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis, in that order.

front: A child has sudden swelling and urine that is mostly albumin. Light microscopy is nearly normal. Electron microscopy shows flattened foot processes.
bottom: The podocyte feet have effaced, and steroids usually restore them.

bullets.clue: Selective albumin loss with bland light microscopy is the pattern.
bullets.treat: A similar adult picture can follow anti-inflammatory drugs. Hodgkin lymphoma is a classic association in some patients.
bullets.trap: Starting cyclophosphamide before a steroid trial in a typical child.

source.recommendation: Minimal change disease is selective proteinuria with foot-process effacement. Children usually respond to steroids.

diagram.alt: Text card. The podocyte feet have effaced, and steroids usually restore them.

front: A diuretic that blocks the triple cotransporter in the thick ascending limb also makes the kidney waste calcium. A different diuretic, acting farther along, saves calcium.
bottom: Loop diuretics waste calcium. Thiazides save it.

bullets.clue: The loop blocks the sodium-potassium-2-chloride transporter and knocks out the drive for paracellular calcium reabsorption.
bullets.treat: Use a loop when calcium is dangerously high. Use a thiazide when calcium stones keep forming.
bullets.trap: Giving a loop diuretic to a patient with recurrent calcium stones and wondering why they continue.

source.recommendation: Loop diuretics inhibit the thick-ascending-limb transporter and increase calcium excretion. Thiazides do the opposite for calcium.

diagram.alt: Text card. Loop diuretics waste calcium. Thiazides save it.

front: An infant has a cleft lip and a malformed ear, and the mother took a vitamin A derivative in the first trimester.
bottom: Neural crest migration into the face and ear was disrupted.

bullets.clue: Isotretinoin is the usual drug. The sensitive window is early, often before a pregnancy is recognized.
bullets.treat: Stop the drug before conception. A pregnancy test and contraception are part of prescribing it.
bullets.trap: Reassuring a patient that a skin drug cannot affect an embryo.

source.recommendation: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen for neural-crest structures of the face and ear.

diagram.alt: Text card. Neural crest migration into the face and ear was disrupted.

front: A tall adolescent has a webbed neck, a coarctation, and streak gonads. The karyotype has one X and no second sex chromosome.
bottom: Turner syndrome, 45,X.

bullets.clue: The lymphatic swelling in fetal life explains the neck and the swollen hands. The ovaries do not develop.
bullets.treat: The extra-X karyotype with small testes, tall stature, and azoospermia is Klinefelter, not this.
bullets.trap: Promising fertility. The streak gonads do not produce eggs.

source.recommendation: Turner syndrome is 45,X. Short stature, webbed neck, coarctation, and streak gonads are the picture. Klinefelter is 47,XXY.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Turner syndrome, 45,X.

front: No sense of smell, and puberty that never starts. The neurons that should have released the puberty hormone never migrated from the olfactory placode.
bottom: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons did not arrive.

bullets.clue: Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are low, and the gonads are quiet because the signal never came.
bullets.treat: This is central. A high gonadotropin with quiet gonads is gonadal failure instead.
bullets.trap: Giving testosterone or estrogen without asking where the signal failed.

source.recommendation: Kallmann syndrome is failed migration of GnRH neurons with the olfactory neurons. Anosmia plus absent puberty is the clue.

diagram.alt: Text card. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons did not arrive.

front: A newborn is virilized and crashing with low sodium and high potassium. The steroid step just before cortisol and aldosterone is blocked, and androgens are overflowing.
bottom: 21-hydroxylase is deficient.

bullets.clue: Cortisol and aldosterone fall. ACTH rises and drives adrenal androgens.
bullets.treat: The salt-wasting form needs both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid. A mild nonclassic form presents later with androgen excess only.
bullets.trap: Treating the potassium and missing the missing cortisol.

source.recommendation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the common congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Salt wasting plus virilization is the severe form.

diagram.alt: Text card. 21-hydroxylase is deficient.

front: Insulin is present, but glucose transporters do not move to the muscle membrane. The transporter that is already in the liver membrane does not need that move.
bottom: GLUT4 needs insulin to reach the muscle and fat membrane. GLUT2 in the liver does not.

bullets.clue: Exercise can move GLUT4 without insulin, which is why muscle still takes up some glucose.
bullets.treat: A drug that raises insulin does nothing useful if the receptor itself is missing, as in severe insulin resistance.
bullets.trap: Saying every glucose transporter waits for insulin.

source.recommendation: GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive transporter of muscle and adipose tissue. Liver GLUT2 is constitutive.

diagram.alt: Text card. GLUT4 needs insulin to reach the muscle and fat membrane. GLUT2 in the liver does not.

front: One hormone raises calcium by bone resorption and kidney reabsorption and activates vitamin D. A second hormone, from the thyroid C cells, lowers calcium.
bottom: Parathyroid hormone raises calcium. Calcitonin lowers it.

bullets.clue: Vitamin D increases gut absorption. Parathyroid hormone's own gut effect is mostly through that activation.
bullets.treat: A high calcium with a high parathyroid hormone is the gland. A high calcium with a low hormone is somewhere else.
bullets.trap: Treating every high calcium as a parathyroid problem.

source.recommendation: Parathyroid hormone and calcitonin move calcium in opposite directions. Vitamin D is the absorption partner.

diagram.alt: Text card. Parathyroid hormone raises calcium. Calcitonin lowers it.

front: A patient keeps making dilute urine even after hours without water. Giving a vasopressin analogue then concentrates the urine. In another patient the analogue does nothing.
bottom: The first lacks the hormone. The second lacks the kidney response.

bullets.clue: Water deprivation should concentrate urine if the axis is intact. Failure that corrects with the analogue is central.
bullets.treat: Lithium and high calcium are classic reasons the kidney stops listening.
bullets.trap: Pouring fluids into a patient who is already losing free water without measuring the urine.

source.recommendation: Central diabetes insipidus responds to desmopressin. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus does not.

diagram.alt: Text card. The first lacks the hormone. The second lacks the kidney response.

front: A patient has high calcium, a pituitary tumor, and a pancreatic endocrine tumor. A different patient has medullary thyroid cancer, a pheochromocytoma, and high calcium from a different gland.
bottom: The first is MEN1. The second is MEN2.

bullets.clue: Menin tumors are parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreas. The ret syndromes add medullary thyroid cancer and pheochromocytoma.
bullets.treat: A pheochromocytoma is removed before any other operation that would stir it. The thyroid cancer in the ret syndromes is medullary, from C cells.
bullets.trap: Mixing the two syndromes and missing the thyroid cancer that has to come out.

source.recommendation: MEN1 is parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreas. MEN2 adds medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.

diagram.alt: Text card. The first is MEN1. The second is MEN2.
